opening.headline: Learn how to solve the problem of not finding documents with the same meaning through keyword search by converting sentences into numeric vectors and comparing them by distance.
body: If a user searches for “how to get a refund,” but the article only says “payment cancellation and return procedures,” the keyword search won’t find any results because none of the words overlap. To a person, it means the same thing, but to a search system, it's a different sentence.

In this class, we will look at why embeddings contain meaning, a measure of distance, tokens and prompt caching, which are common units of cost, model and dimension information from the documents of the three companies and external providers, the impact of task types and dimensions on quality and cost, why vector search indexes are fast, and quantization. Next, we check cases of rapid increases in storage costs and multilingual queries, and explain the indicators that compare search quality numerically.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain embedding, dimensionality, similarity, and vector search
It can explain the learning principle that embedding contains meaning and the relationship between cosine, dot product, and L2 scale.
Describe how tokens, context windows, and prompt caching affect limits and costs
Distinguish how task types and dimensions impact search quality and cost
This explains why approximate search is fast and the cost of recall.
Explain how to compare search quality with recall@k and MRR

screens.title: You cannot find documents with the same meaning through keyword search.
screens.lead: Read the question you entered in the search box and the sentences in the document side by side. Compare two sentences with different words but the same meaning and think about what the problem is.

visual.alt: I entered 'refund method' in the search box, but there were 0 results, and next to it I saw the missed document 'Payment Cancellation and Return Procedure'.

paragraphs: We created a function to search customer center documents. The user entered "refund method" into the search bar. However, the document only says “Payment cancellation and return procedures.”

Keyword search checks whether the entered word is included in the document. There are no overlapping words in the two sentences, so the result is 0. What happens is that even though the information the user is looking for is clearly there, they cannot find it.
You can force users to change search terms and re-enter them. However, a good search should compare meaning, not words. How can we find documents with the same meaning? This class covers how.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: For a computer to calculate that the meanings of two sentences are close, what form should the meanings be changed to? Find the answer as you progress through class.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that we need a way to compare meanings instead of words, let's start by recalling your own experience.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to change your search term several times to find the document you wanted?
items.answer: When a user changes words to match the expression written in the document, it is like leaving the search system's job to the user. Comparative semantic searches reduce this burden.

items.prompt: Think of the concept of similar points on a map.
items.answer: On the map, if the distance is close, the location is similar. Embedding transfers this concept to meaning. Sentences are expressed with numbers like coordinates, and if the distance between two sentences is close, the meaning is considered close.

items.prompt: Was there a moment when you asked a question in Korean and it would have been nice to find information in English?
items.answer: Even if the languages are different, if the meaning is the same, it is possible if there is a semantic space located in the same place. An embedding model that supports multiple languages ​​aims at this, and is covered as an example later in the lesson.

screens.outro: Let's transfer the concept of distance from a map into semantic space. First, let's check what an embedding is.

screens.title: What is Embedding?
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation will appear. Check the terms one by one and try to connect them with the distance concept on the dot map on the right.

visual.alt: A drawing in which sentences are placed closer or further apart depending on their meaning on a two-dimensional dot map.
labels: What is the meaning of life?
What is the purpose of existence?
The actual embedding has hundreds of dimensions, and the picture is simplified to 2 dimensions.

data.text: Embedding consists of a list of floating-point numbers, i.e., vector. The The closer the distance, the higher the relevance. between two vector have lower similarity the farther apart they are. In the document's example, "What is the meaning of life?" and "What is the purpose of existence?" are placed close together, while "How to bake a cake" is positioned far away. The number of numerical values possessed by vector is referred to as number of dimensions, and a paragraph can be represented by hundreds of dimensions of vector. Embedding is used in search, Clustering, recommendation, Anomaly detection, and classification. Even though the words "refund method" and "payment cancellation and return procedure" differ, they are placed close together in vector.

terms.tip: A list of floating point numbers. An embedding represents the meaning of a sentence or image as this list of numbers.

terms.term: The closer the distance, the higher the relevance.
terms.tip: A short distance between two vectors means they have similar meanings. Searching involves finding document vectors that are close to the question vector.
The number of numbers the vector has, i.e. the length of the vector. Higher dimensions allow for richer expressions, but increase storage and computation costs.
This is a task of grouping similar vectors together. It is used for classifying document topics or grouping customer opinions.
The task is to find items that are far away from other vectors. It is used to filter out unusual documents or records.

screens.title: Why embeddings are meaningful and similarity measures
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how the embedding is learned and how the closeness of two vectors is measured. In the final tab we see why changing the model requires recreating all of the vectors.

tabs.label: learning intuition
tabs.body:
Embedding models are not created by humans defining meaning through calculations, but are the result of learning from many examples. One of the methods used for learning is contrastive learning. We adjust the model slightly so that related pairs (e.g. a question and a document that answers the question) have vectors closer together, and unrelated pairs have vectors farther apart. By repeating this adjustment for a very large number of pairs, sentences with similar meanings are clustered close together in space.

The reason why “refund method” and “payment cancellation and return procedure” are close is not because the words are the same, but because expressions that have the same meaning have been taught to be placed close together. Sentence-BERT, which learns by comparing sentence pairs, Dense Passage Retrieval, which searches questions and documents by converting them into vectors, and text/code embedding research using contrastive learning with large-scale unsupervised data demonstrate this approach.

tabs.label: Cosine, dot product, L2
tabs.body:
There are three representative measures to measure whether two vectors are close.

- **Cosine Similarity**: See how similar the directions the two vectors are pointing are. Values ​​range from -1 to 1, with larger values ​​being similar.
- **Dot Product**: In addition to the direction, it also reflects the length of the vector.
- **L2 Distance**: The straight line distance between two points, the smaller the closer.

If we normalize the vector to length 1, the three measures will have the same rank. If the length is 1, the cosine similarity and the dot product are the same, and the square of the L2 distance is 2 minus twice the dot product, so the larger the dot product, the smaller the distance. So, in normalized embedding, the search ranking is the same no matter which measure is used. For non-normalized vectors, the ranking may vary depending on the scale, so follow the scale recommended in the model documentation. For example, the Gemini documentation advises that vectors reduced to dimensions other than 3072 in gemini-embedding-001 should be normalized manually.

tabs.label: Compare only in the same space
tabs.body:
Query vectors and document vectors must be created by the same model to be compared. This is because the axes of the semantic space are learned differently for each model. Even if the number of dimensions is coincidentally the same, the numbers from one model and the numbers from another model are not on the same basis, so the distances have no meaning if they are mixed and compared.

Here are two practical rules: First, when embedding a query, the same model used in the document is used. Second, if you change the embedding model, all previously saved document vectors must be recreated with the new model. The more documents there are, the greater the cost of this re-bedding, so replacing a model is a decision that must factor in not only performance but also the cost of rebuilding it.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the principle of distance between meaning, let us summarize the tokens, which are the units of cost and limit used throughout this process.

ext.title: Reimers & Gurevych, Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
Karpukhin et al., Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
Neelakantan et al., Text and Code Embeddings by Contrastive Pre-Training

screens.title: Basics of token, context window, and prompt caching
screens.lead: Most model limits and costs are calculated in units called tokens. Select the right arrow to follow the sequence from text to token, to context window, to rates, and to caching prompts.

steps.title: 1. Text is split into tokens
steps.body: The model does not read letters or words as they are, but in pieces called tokens. Many models divide text into subwords that take frequent sets of characters into single pieces, with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) being a representative algorithm. Common words are divided into one token, rare words are divided into multiple tokens. In English text, a rough estimate is that four characters equal one token, but this is not an exact value because the tokenization method varies from model to model.

steps.title: 2. The number of tokens is different for each language.
steps.body: Even in sentences with the same meaning, the number of tokens varies depending on the tokenization method of the language and model. Less common letter combinations in the training data tend to be split into smaller pieces, so Korean often costs more tokens than English for the same content. Therefore, rather than calculating limits and costs for Korean documents based on English estimates, calculate them directly using the token calculation function of the model you are using.

steps.title: 3. The context window is limited to being shared between input and output.
steps.body: The context window is the total amount of tokens the model can handle in one call. This limit is shared between the input, which consists of directives, documents, and conversation records, and the new output that the model creates. When the input almost fills the window, there is no room for output, and input that exceeds the window must be reduced or split and sent. The maximum number of input tokens for an embedding model is also a limit, indicating the length of text that can be converted into a vector at one time.

steps.title: 4. Fees are also based on tokens.
steps.body: Model call fees are calculated based on the number of tokens processed. Calls that generate text usually have separate input and output tokens calculated, and the unit cost varies depending on the model and provider. Embeddings are calculated only for input tokens. So, if you put the same long document in the input for each call, the input tokens will stack up to the length of the document multiplied by the number of calls. This multiplication is the biggest reason why long context methods increase the cost.

steps.title: 5. Prompt caching does not recalculate the same prefix
steps.body:
Prompt caching is a function that stores the first part of a prompt that has already been processed and reuses it without recalculating the same first part in the next call. In this case, the unit is the prefix that continues from the beginning of the prompt, and to be reused, the part must be identical down to the letter. Claude's documentation explains that prefixes that lead to tool definitions, system instructions, and message sequences are cache targets, and that if the contents of the preceding ones change, the subsequent cache becomes invalid.

Therefore, to be effective, put content that doesn't change (directives, large documents) first and content that changes from call to call (user questions) last. Cache has a limited retention time, so it is less effective in services where queries for the same document are infrequent.

steps.title: 6. These numbers are all in the same units
steps.body: The maximum input of the embedding model, the judgment on the size of the entire document, the throughput according to the number of images and PDF pages, and the cost of calling SQL functions are all connected to the same unit called a token. When you come across a number, first read it to determine whether this value is an input limit, the size of the window shared between input and output, or the unit for calculating the fee. If you read without distinction, requests that you thought were within the limit will fail due to insufficient output space, or you will receive a larger bill than expected.

data.notes: The criteria for choosing a model are how well it fits the size and domain of my data, inference performance, and whether it is customizable. Even models with the same name may have different dimension options, so check the documentation for the model you are using to see what values ​​are supported. Additionally, embedding fees are charged based on the number of tokens entered, so the more documents you have, the more embedding costs you will need to factor into your calculations. It is common to save and reuse vectors once created, and the cost also includes the need to recreate all vectors when the model is changed. What the MTEB assessment performance in the table means and how to interpret it is covered in this lesson's Search Quality commentary.

screens.title: Impact of task type and dimension
screens.lead: Try changing the dimension values with the sliders to see the effect on storage size and quality. We also look at why dimensions can be cut and used and why task types are important.

visual.alt: A graph where the bars representing the vector storage size grow longer depending on the dimension value.
labels: Select only values supported by the model

stops.body: It is the smallest dimension. The storage space occupied by one vector is small and comparison calculations are fast. Instead, it can be less expressive, allowing review when documents are very numerous and subtle semantic differences are not important. A value must be supported by the model to be selected.

It's one of those mid-points between cost and quality. If the model provides a parameter to reduce dimensionality, you can save storage and calculations by reducing it from 3072 or 1536 to 512. Search quality before and after reduction should be checked by comparing the same set of queries.

This is the default dimension used by Voyage's voyage-4, voyage-4-large, and voyage-4-lite. This is a reasonable value to balance expressiveness and cost. When calculating similarity, cosine similarity is often used, as shown in the example in the document.

This is a large dimension used when richer expression is needed. Storage and computation costs increase, so if there are a large number of documents, the burden increases quickly. Dimensions can only be selected from values ​​supported by the model.

The reason that the dimensionality can be reduced to `dimensions` or `output_dimensionality` is because these models were trained in a way called Matryoshka representation learning. To ensure that small expressions are contained within large expressions, like a Russian doll, information about the big picture is first placed in the front dimension of the vector, and detailed information is added to the back dimension. So, even if you cut off the back, a usable expression remains with just the front, and the quality gradually decreases rather than drastically. OpenAI's announcement and Gemini documentation reveal that they use this method.

If you truncate the vectors of an untrained model at random locations, important information may be scattered behind them, greatly reducing quality. This is the reason for the rule that dimensions should only be selected from values ​​supported by the model. After truncation, normalization may be required to reset the length to 1, depending on the model documentation.

Gemini's gemini-embedding-001 is `task_type`, which can tell you about uses like SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY, RETRIEVAL_QUERY, and RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT. gemini-embedding-2 strongly recommends that when working with text, you prefix your prompts with an operation prefix appropriate to your query and document. Even if the same sentence is used separately for search queries and documents, the quality can be improved. Since questions and documents have different lengths and characteristics, it is helpful to tell the model what role the vectors will be used for.

screens.title: Why Vector Indexes Are Fast: Approximate Search and Recall
screens.lead: Selecting the number marker above the picture shows how vector searches can be made faster and at what cost. Please check them one by one starting from number 1.

visual.alt: Illustration showing a comparison between exhaustive comparison and layered graph exploration, and combining ranks with missed neighbors.
labels: Total comparison (proportional to the number of documents)

markers.label: Total comparison
markers.title: Measuring all vectors and distances is accurate but slow.
markers.body: By calculating the distance between the query vector and all stored document vectors one by one, you can find the closest item exactly. However, the amount of computation is proportional to the number of documents. If there are tens of millions of documents, tens of millions of distance calculations are needed for each query, and the higher the dimension, the heavier even a single calculation becomes. It is difficult to meet the response time of the search screen where people are waiting. This method of finding accurate nearest neighbors is called exact search.

markers.label: Graph navigation
markers.title: Approximate search to find nearby items by visiting only a few
markers.body: An approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search finds nearby items by visiting only some of them rather than looking at all of them. The representative HNSW method stacks several layers of graphs in which nearby vectors are connected by lines. It jumps large distances in the sparsely connected upper layer to move to the vicinity of the query, and then searches for neighbors in detail in the densely connected lower layer. The paper explains that the search cost scales approximately logarithmically with data size. The same idea is to divide the vector into bundles and examine only the bundles that are close to the query.

markers.label: recall rate
markers.title: You can miss out on your real neighbors for a quick price.
markers.body: Only a few are visited, so you might miss out on the ones that are truly closest to you. The proportion of the top k items that are really close that the search actually finds is called recall. Setting more candidates to visit increases recall, but at the expense of time. This balance between speed and accuracy is the key to indexing. Since the setting name and default value are different for each product, check the documentation for the product you are using for items that control the number of candidates.

markers.label: regrade
markers.title: Get a wide range of candidates using compressed vectors and recalculate them.
markers.body: Compressing vectors with quantization can result in coarser distance calculations, further reducing recall. So, oversampling brings in more candidates than needed, and rescoring corrects the ranking by recalculating the distances for those candidates with a vector of original precision. It is a two-stage structure that reduces candidates in a fast, rough stage and orders them in a slow, but precise stage. Knowing this structure helps us understand why oversampling and rescoring are used together with quantization.

markers.label: Combine ranks
markers.title: Combine keyword results and vector results into one
markers.body: In hybrid search, keyword search and vector search have different units of relevance values, so they cannot be added directly. Reciprocal rank join (RRF) uses the rank in each list instead of the value. For each document, the quotient of 1 divided by (the rank plus a constant) is added to the list's rank, and the total is sorted in order of largest total. The original paper used 60 as the constant. In both lists, higher-ranking documents move up. Keyword rankings are often performed using a word frequency-based ranking function such as BM25.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principles of approximate search, let's compare the original vector and the quantized vector.

ext.title: Malkov & Yashunin, Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
Cormack, Clarke, Buettcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods (SIGIR 2009)

screens.title: Vector search index and quantization
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the difference between saving the original vector as is and quantizing it.

visual.alt: Diagram of indexing vectors from the original table and index size bars before and after quantization.

states.label: original float32
states.body: The vector search index indexes vectors in the source table and finds items close to the query. Databricks AI Search provides real-time similarity search on top of sources such as delta tables, and supports hybrid search, filters, and reranking. Source tables have requirements such as serverless or change data feeds. Storing vectors at their native precision provides the best quality, but the more documents you have, the greater the storage and memory costs.

states.label: Quantization
states.body: Azure AI Search supports scalar (int8) quantization and binary quantization, with int8 reducing the index size by a factor of 1 and binary quantization by up to 28 times. Binary quantization is particularly effective for embeddings with dimensions greater than 1024, the document explains. Quantization is a lossy compression that reduces the precision of numbers. The impact is reduced by oversampling and rescoring. That is, after getting enough candidates, recalculate them with a vector of the original precision to correct the ranking.

screens.outro: Now, let's take a look at the case where storage costs have increased rapidly.

screens.title: Commentary: A case of skyrocketing storage costs
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of reducing the cost of indexing 10 million document chunks. Select the right arrow to apply the steps one by one and follow the cost bar as it decreases.

visual.alt: Bar graph with index size decreasing at each step.
labels: Quality improvement through oversampling and rescoring
Compare quality with the same set of queries

steps.title: situation
steps.body: When we indexed 10 million document chunks with 3072-dimensional float32, memory and disk costs skyrocketed. One vector is 3072 real numbers, so 10 million is a lot of numbers to store. The goal is to maintain search quality while reducing costs.

steps.title: Step 1: Reduce the dimensions first
steps.body: If your model supports it, reduce the vector length by reducing the dimension to 1024 or 512. OpenAI's `dimensions` parameter provides this function. Remember that dimensions can only be chosen from values ​​supported by the model.

steps.title: Step 2: Quantize int8 scalar
steps.body: Int8 scalar quantization reduces the size by about a quarter. This may affect quality as it reduces the precision of the numbers. However, it is a method worth trying first because the loss is relatively small.

steps.title: Step 3: Binary Quantization if Greater Savings Are Needed
steps.body: If greater savings are needed, use binary quantization. Although the size is greatly reduced, the loss also increases, so the quality loss is compensated by oversampling and rescoring. This is a method that finds enough candidates and then recalculates the ranking using precise vectors.

steps.title: Step 4: Compare before and after reduction
steps.body: Whichever method you use, compare the search quality before and after reduction for the same set of queries. Just reducing costs is not enough to call it a success. In important queries, you need to check with numbers whether the results have deteriorated.

steps.title: Reason for order
steps.body: We apply the method with the smallest loss first, use the method with the larger loss when greater savings are needed, and check the quality at the end. If you try to make big savings first, it is difficult to know at what stage the quality decline is caused.

screens.title: Commentary: Multilingual Queries and Hybrid Search
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of finding English documents using Korean queries. Select the right arrows to follow the steps: Query, Embed, Candidate, and Rerank.

visual.alt: A flow in which Korean queries and English documents are placed in the same semantic space and combined with keyword search to re-rank.

steps.title: 1. Korean query, English document
steps.body: I am trying to find the English document "Refund policy" with the Korean query "Refund method". The two sentences are written in different languages, so no word overlaps. No matter what method you use, you won't be able to connect by keyword search.

steps.title: 2. Put multilingual embeddings in the same space
steps.body: Multilingual embedding places the same meaning in different languages in close locations in the same semantic space. Then, the distance between the query vector and the English document vector becomes closer, so you can find it. Multilingual support models such as gemini-embedding-2 and voyage-4 are models aimed at such cross-language search.

steps.title: 3. When keywords are more precise
steps.body: For product codes and proper nouns, literal agreement is more important than meaning. For example, a search for your model number should not return any other numbers that are semantically similar. In this case, a hybrid search that mixes keyword search and vector search is helpful.

steps.title: 4. Increase precision by re-ranking
steps.body: Precision increases by re-ordering the candidates collected from both methods. Some services, like Databricks AI Search, support hybrid search, filters, and re-ranking.

steps.title: 5. Quality is confirmed through actual inquiry.
steps.body: Rather than deciding which configuration is best by feeling, it is checked by comparing it with a collection of actual queries. It should contain a variety of frequently asked questions about the service, questions with mixed languages, and questions that include code. A collection of queries is created once, and each time the model, dimension, or quantization method is changed, the same collection is returned and compared. The indicators used for comparison, recall@k and MRR, are explained in detail in the following screen.

screens.title: Commentary: How to compare search quality numerically
screens.lead: The instructor explains what the phrase “comparing with the same set of queries” specifically means. Select each tab to see a set of queries, two leading metrics, and how to read public benchmarks. All calculation examples are assumptions for illustrative purposes only.

tabs.label: collection of queries
tabs.body: To compare search quality, you first need a collection of queries and the correct documents that answer the query. The actual questions are pulled from the service log and humans mark the correct answers in the document. It contains frequently asked questions, questions with mixed languages, and questions containing product codes. By keeping this collection fixed, you can compare results using the same criteria whenever you change the embedding model, dimension, quantization, or index settings. If you input only a few questions without a collection and make your decision, it is easy to be drawn to a case that happened to be good.

tabs.label: recall@k
tabs.body:
For each query, recall@k checks whether the correct document is included in the top k search results and calculates the percentage of queries that were included.

Example assumption: If 7 out of 10 queries had the correct document in the top 5, recall@5 would be 7/10, or 0.7.

The top k are also candidates to pass to the model. If the correct answer document is not shortlisted, the correct answer cannot be used no matter how good the subsequent re-ranking or creation steps are. So recall@k is a basic indicator to see if the search step doesn't miss the correct answer. For queries with multiple correct answers, a definition is used to calculate the ratio of the correct answers found.

tabs.label: MRR and nDCG
tabs.body:
recall@k considers the 1st or 5th place the same as long as the correct answer is within k numbers. The indicator that even reflects the order is MRR. If r is the rank of the first correct answer for each query, 1/r is calculated and averaged across all queries.

Hypothetical example: If the correct answers to three questions are ranked 1st, 2nd, and 4th respectively, the average of 1, 1/2, and 1/4 is approximately 0.58. The higher the correct answer, the larger the value.

nDCG is an indicator used when the degree of relevance of the correct answer is at various levels (very relevant, somewhat relevant, etc.). The higher the level of relevance, the higher the value is given to the document, and the lower the contribution, the lower the contribution.

tabs.label: How to read benchmarks
tabs.body:
MTEB is a public benchmark that collects datasets from many languages and multiple task types, such as classification, clustering, and search, and compares embedding models all at once. The paper covers eight task types, 58 datasets, and 112 languages, and reports that no single method was best for all tasks. BEIR is a benchmark that measures how well a search model generalizes across multiple domains of data it has never seen before.

Therefore, the MTEB values ​​in the table should be used as a starting point for inferring candidate models, and the final selection should be checked again in the query collection containing my document, my language, and my question. There is no guarantee that the rankings in public benchmarks will be the same in your domain.

screens.outro: Now that we have the indicators, we will organize the contents of this class into one.

ext.title: Muennighoff et al., MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
Thakur et al., BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models

screens.title: Change meaning to distance and look at cost and quality together
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first refund method example and tie the content of this lesson together.

paragraphs: The first problem was that if the words did not overlap, documents with the same meaning could not be found. Embedding turns text or images into numeric vectors, with the distance between vectors indicating closeness of meaning. So you can link “Refund Method” and “Payment Cancellation and Return Procedure”.

Higher dimensions provide richer representations but increase storage and retrieval costs. Some models provide parameters to reduce dimensionality. Models that support task types (task_type) or task prefixes, such as Gemini, allow you to obtain embeddings suitable for purposes such as search, classification, and similarity.

Vector search index is an approximate search that quickly finds items close to the query during embedding, at the cost of slightly lower recall. Hybrid search mixed with keyword search is also possible. Quantization significantly reduces storage costs by compressing vectors to int8 or 1 bit, and the multilingual model allows Korean queries to find English documents. No matter what you choose, the rule is to check the quality by comparing the before and after reduction with the same set of queries.

In practice, creating a collection of queries is surprisingly the biggest task. By pulling actual questions from your service logs and pairing them with answers, you can quantify every subsequent choice with metrics like recall@k and MRR. Knowing why embeddings are meaningful, that tokens are units of cost, and that approximate search trades speed for recall makes it clear what to look for when reading the numbers in a model document.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Embedded searches complement keyword searches, not replace them. Which is better depends on the nature of the query. Please review the service inquiries yourself and make your own judgment. If proper nouns and codes are important to your service, consider hybrid.

glossary.def: This is an expression that converts text, etc. into a numeric vector containing meaning. The number of numbers a vector has is called its dimension.
A piece-by-piece at which the model reads text and calculates rates. The size of the context window and the cost of the call are determined by the number of tokens.
It is a measure of how similar the directions pointed by two vectors are. Normalizing a vector gives the same rank as the dot product.
This is a technique to reduce the size by compressing the number of vectors with low precision.
This is the percentage of truly close or correct documents that the search actually found. This is a value that is exchanged for the speed of approximate search.
This method uses keyword search and vector similarity search together. It is common to combine the two results based on ranking.

misconceptions.myth: With embedding, there is no need for keyword search.
misconceptions.fact: For queries where literal matching is important, such as product codes or proper nouns, keywords are accurate. Hybrid searches that mix both methods are often advantageous.

misconceptions.myth: The higher the level, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Higher dimensions allow for richer expressions, but increase storage and computation costs. You need to find a balance that suits your service, and some models provide parameters to reduce dimensionality.

misconceptions.myth: When quantized, the quality inevitably drops significantly.
misconceptions.fact: Since this is lossy compression, it does have an impact, but can be reduced with oversampling and rescoring. The actual impact must be measured against the same set of queries.

misconceptions.myth: Vector search compares all documents and always finds the correct neighbors.
misconceptions.fact: For large indexes, we use a partial-visit approximate search for speed. So sometimes it misses its true neighbors, and this is adjusted to the stock setting as recall.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Embedding is the conversion of text or images into numeric vectors, and is the result of learning to keep similar pairs close together, so the distance between vectors indicates closeness in meaning.

Since queries and documents must be compared in the space of the same model, if the model is changed, all vectors must be recreated, and the dimensionality is reduced within the values supported by the model learned using the Matryoshka method.
Tokens are a common unit of limits and costs, and in models that support task types or prefixes, such as Gemini's task_type, you can get an embedding that suits your purposes.
The vector search index sacrifices some recall at the expense of quickly finding neighbors through approximate search, and allows for a hybrid of keyword search and ranking-based merging.

Quantization reduces storage costs and is complemented by oversampling and rescoring, and all choices are checked by comparing before and after reduction on the same set of queries with metrics such as recall@k and MRR.

closing.reflection: What documents in my document repository could I have found by semantics but not by keyword?

checks.q: I searched for “refund method,” but the only document I found was “payment cancellation and return procedure.” Why can an embedding search find this document?
options: This is because sentences with similar meanings are located close to each other in the vector space.
This is because ranking is done by counting the degree to which words overlap.
This is because only files with the same document title are selected.
This is because if the number of dimensions of the vectors is the same, they are always considered related.
checks.explain: Embedding turns the meaning into a floating point vector, and the closer the distance, the more relevant it is.

wrong.1: That's how keyword search works and here words don't overlap.
wrong.2: An embedding expresses the meaning, not the title, as a vector of numbers.
wrong.3: The number of dimensions is just the length of the vector, and relevance is seen as the distance between vectors.

checks.q: Users ask questions about the same long internal regulatory documents hundreds of times a day. How should I configure my prompts to get the best benefit from prompt caching?
options: For each call, the current time and user question are placed at the beginning of the prompt, followed by the document.
Insert user questions into the middle of the document to provide context.
Always place directives and prescriptive documents in the same order, first before the prompt, with user questions last.
Documents are shuffled in a different order for each call so the cache is created fresh each time.
checks.explain: The cache is only reused when the prefixes leading from the beginning of the prompt are exactly the same. Content that does not change should be placed at the front and content that changes between calls should be placed at the end to avoid recalculating long documents.

wrong.0: If the content at the beginning changes every time, the prefixes of subsequent documents also change, so the cache cannot be used.
wrong.1: If a question is placed in the middle of a document, the content following the question must be recalculated on each call.
wrong.3: If you change the order, the prefix will be different and the cache will not be hit.

checks.q: What happens if we reduce the embedding dimension from 3072 to 512?
options: Storage costs only increase, but expressiveness remains the same.
The dimension can be freely chosen to be any value.
Storage and computation costs are reduced, but expressiveness may be lowered, so search quality must be checked.
Quality always improves and there are no downsides
checks.explain: Since dimensionality reduction is a matter of balancing cost and quality, we compare before and after reduction for the same set of queries.

wrong.0: Reducing dimensionality means less storage and computation.
wrong.1: Dimensions are chosen only from those values supported by the model.
wrong.3: This may result in lower expressiveness, so a balance is needed.

checks.q: Services with tens of millions of document vectors use approximate nearest neighbor search. What is an appropriate explanation for this choice?
options: It measures all vectors and distances, so it is always accurate, but the cost is high.
Instead of speeding up response by only visiting some parts, you may occasionally miss items that are really close, and that degree is measured by recall rate.
Quantization changes approximate search into exact search, so the recall rate is always 100%.
When mixed with keyword search, the errors of approximate search completely disappear.
checks.explain: Approximate search comes at the price of recall by reducing the range of visits for speed. Increasing the number of candidates increases recall at the expense of time.

wrong.0: That's the description of exact search, and with a large number of documents it is difficult to meet response time requirements.
wrong.2: Quantization is a compression that reduces size and can actually affect recall.
wrong.3: Hybridization is just a way to combine different strengths and does not eliminate the omissions of approximate search.

checks.q: Guess the order of document chunks to reduce the cost of storing 10 million vectors
items: Reduce the dimensionality to 1024 or 512 if your model supports it.
int8 scalar quantization reduces size by about a quarter
If greater savings are needed, use binary quantization and oversampling/rescoring.
Compare search quality before and after reduction for the same set of queries.
checks.explain: We apply the method with the smallest loss first, use binary quantization when larger savings are needed, and check at the end to make sure there is no quality loss.

checks.q: The embedding model with the highest MTEB average was selected as the candidate. What is the best thing to do before making a final choice?
options: Since it has the highest public ranking, I see it as the best for my service and confirm it right away.
Compare recall@k and MRR between candidate models in a collection of queries created from my documents and my questions.
The model with the largest dimension is always better, so compare only the dimensions.
Enter one or two queries directly and see if the results are plausible.
checks.explain: Public benchmarks are the starting point for model reasoning. Different domains, languages, and question types can result in different rankings, so you should compare metrics from the same set of queries.

wrong.0: Public benchmarks do not guarantee the performance of your domain.
wrong.2: Larger dimensions are not always better and also increase storage and computation costs.
wrong.3: Just a few questions won't reduce the impact of chance.
